title: Fixing 404 Not Found Errors: An In-Depth Technical Guide to Crawl Budget and User Experience
content:
In technical SEO, error codes are not just passing messages a visitor happens to see. They are vital signs that show how healthy a website’s infrastructure looks to search engine crawlers. One code stands out among them as one of the most common errors, and one of the most damaging to user experience and to a site’s reputation with Google: the 404 Not Found error.


In this comprehensive, up-to-date guide from SEO House, we take the problem apart from an advanced technical angle, well beyond the surface, and give you the monitoring, analysis and root-cause fixes we apply for our own clients.

1. Decoding the Code: What Does a 404 Error Mean Technically?

Before getting into solutions, we first need to understand what error 404 actually means and how the server reads it. The code is one of the HTTP status codes defined by the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, and it belongs to the 4xx family of client-side errors.


404 in a nutshell: the client (a browser or a search engine crawler) connected to the server successfully, but the server could not find the requested file or page in the database or at the specified path, or the server is configured to withhold that information without pointing to an alternative.


Historically and technically, the code is made up of three digits, each with its own meaning:

  • The first 4: indicates that the error is on the client side (for example, a mistyped URL or a deleted page).
  • The middle 0: indicates a general syntax or protocol-level error.
  • The last 4: pinpoints the specific condition, “resource not found” (Not Found).

3. Managing 404 Errors in Online Stores (Shopify, Zid, Salla)

Having managed many large online stores in the Gulf market on platforms such as Shopify, Zid and Salla, we see that 404 errors most often come from how out-of-stock products are handled. The golden rule: do not delete a product the moment it sells out.

  • Temporarily out of stock: do not delete the page or redirect it. Let the page keep returning 200 OK, and show the visitor a clear “Out of stock” message with a “Notify me when available” option.
  • Permanently discontinued: here we use a 301 redirect to the closest alternative product or to the parent category page, to pass on link juice and keep the traffic.
  • Changing category URLs: when you run a migration or change URL structures on platforms such as Salla or Zid, make sure URL redirects are set up from the dashboard before the changes go live.

4. The Real Impact of 404 Errors on SEO

  • Crawl budget waste: when crawlers follow dead links and hit a 404 code, you spend that budget on pages with no value.
  • Damaged user experience (UX) and a higher bounce rate: the visitor’s instinctive reaction is to close the tab and go back to the search results (pogo-sticking), which sends strong negative signals to Google’s algorithms.
  • Lost link juice: if a strong backlink points to a page that now returns 404, the value of that backlink is lost entirely.

5. How to Detect 404 Errors (Expert Tools)

At SEO House, we rely on a multi-layered monitoring strategy:

  • Google Search Console: the official tool. In the Pages report, we review the pages listed as “Not found (404)” and “Soft 404”.
  • Screaming Frog SEO Spider: a full crawl of the site to find broken internal and external links and trace where they come from (inlinks).
  • Log file analysis: to see precisely when and how Googlebot runs into 404 pages, an advanced technique for large websites.

6. The Technical Fixes We Use at SEO House

1- Smart One-to-One Redirects (301 Redirect)

If the page has strong traffic or backlinks, redirect it with a 301 to the closest directly relevant page.

# Example redirect in an .htaccess file
Redirect 301 /old-product-page
https://www.yourdomain.com/new-product-category

2- Let the 404 Breathe (Natural Removal)

If you have deleted a page permanently, it has no replacement, and it had no backlinks or meaningful traffic, it is healthy to leave the 404 code in place so Google gradually removes the page from its index.

3- Use a 410 (Gone) Code for Immediate, Permanent Removal

If you want to speed up the complete removal of a page from Google’s index, you can use a 410 Gone response. This code sends search crawlers a clear, unambiguous signal that the page was deliberately deleted and will not come back. Once Google reads this code, it drops the URL from its index much faster than it would with a regular 404, which saves crawl budget right away.

4- Design a Custom 404 Page That Serves the User

Since 404 errors are unavoidable, design a 404 page that includes:

  • A friendly, clear explanation that the page does not exist.
  • A smart search bar.
  • Links to the site’s main sections and best-selling products.

7. Conclusion: 404 Errors Are Not the End, but a Chance to Improve

Ultimately, 404 errors are not a disaster in themselves. They are a natural part of the life cycle of any dynamic website or online store that keeps growing and evolving. The secret lies in how you manage them and how intelligently you guide crawlers, so the budget allocated to your site is not wasted. At SEO House, we believe continuous monitoring and regular maintenance are what separate a site that gradually loses visitors to broken links from one that turns every error into a chance to improve user experience and hold on to its top rankings.

To help you apply these strategies consistently and in practice, we have put together the checklist below as a standing reference for you and your development team.

8. A Quick Checklist for Website Managers

We recommend that our team and our clients follow this routine:

  • Never delete expired products without a redirect plan (301).
  • Check the site’s internal links after any URL migration.
  • Make sure the custom 404 page does not return a 200 OK code, but an explicit 404.
